# Incident automation rollout review

I need a decision memo for Monday's operations review on whether we should expand the Assist workflow to the rest of the company.

We enabled Assist for both pilot service groups at 00:00 UTC on June 8 after one week on the manual workflow.

There was no holdout because the service owners wanted a single cutover, but they regard the before-and-after comparison as clean because every pilot incident followed the workflow active when it opened.

Please determine whether Assist caused faster recovery, estimate how many responder-hours we can credibly attribute to it, and recommend whether the evidence supports expansion.

The frozen local exports are in this directory:

- `incidents.csv` contains every incident opened from June 1 through June 14.
- `activity.csv` contains the recorded resolution activity as of the extract.
- `staffing.csv` contains the daily operating snapshot for each service group.

The extract was taken at 23:59 UTC on June 22, so even the newest incidents had at least seven full days to mature.

Use time to close and responder minutes as the primary outcomes, but check whether the recommendation is consistent with the other fields.

Leadership needs the result today, so work from these local exports only and state clearly what the data can and cannot establish.

/bin/zsh -lc "cat > decision-memo.md <<'EOF'
# Assist expansion decision | Monday operations review

**Defer company-wide expansion and book 0 responder-hours of savings.** The pilot does not identify Assist’s causal effect because both groups switched on the same date and operating conditions changed at the cutover. The observable evidence points toward slower closure and higher labor for comparable incidents. Against the manual week’s rates for a comparable case mix, Assist cases with recorded closures used about **102 additional responder-hours**. Treat that as a descriptive comparison, with the causal number of hours saved or added unknown.

## Recovery

All 420 incidents were assigned by UTC opening time, with 210 in each week and 105 per service group per week. Workflow labels agreed with the June 8 cutover, and daily incident counts agreed with staffing. The incident-to-activity join retained all openings. There were 209 manual and 200 Assist closure records. Each incident had at least seven days of follow-up, and all recorded closures occurred within seven days. Missing activity means **no recorded closure** and could reflect unresolved work or incomplete capture.

The dashboard’s closed-case median fell from **436 to 326.5 minutes**. Including all openings and placing incidents without a recorded close at the seven-day horizon still gives a lower pooled median, **436 to 330 minutes**. The mix changed sharply. Sev3 rose from **47% to 73%** of openings, while sev1 and sev2 each halved in count. Every severity tier moved in the opposite direction from the pooled median.

| Severity | Opened, manual → Assist | Median minutes to recorded close, manual → Assist¹ | Recorded closed by day 7, manual → Assist | Mean responder minutes per recorded closure, manual → Assist |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Sev1 | 28 → 14 | 1,100 → 1,768 | 28/28 → 9/14 | 240.0 → 312.2 |
| Sev2 | 84 → 42 | 512.5 → 744.5 | 84/84 → 40/42 | 99.2 → 137.3 |
| Sev3 | 98 → 154 | 167.5 → 303 | 97/98 → 151/154 | 39.2 → 65.4 |

¹ All openings included. Time is capped at seven days, assigning seven days to incidents with no recorded closure.

Overall, **209/210 manual versus 191/210 Assist** incidents had a recorded closure within 24 hours, and **209/210 versus 200/210** within seven days. Mean time without a recorded close over the first seven days rose from **474 to 910 minutes**, or from **403 to 910 minutes** after reweighting manual incidents to the Assist distribution of service group, severity, and intake channel. The similarly reweighted manual median was **197 minutes**, versus **330** for Assist. Even capping follow-up at 24 hours gives a higher unadjusted mean for Assist, **488 versus 433 minutes**. Among recorded closures, mean elapsed time and mean labor were higher in every service-by-severity-by-channel cell with closure records in both weeks (16 of 18 cells).

## Responder-hours and quality

Finance’s conversion from elapsed time to savings has no labor basis in these records. Elapsed time and responder minutes measure different things. Recorded labor totaled **314.3 manual hours versus 302.9 Assist hours**, an apparent 11.4-hour reduction with nine fewer closure records and many more sev3 openings. Mean labor per recorded closure was **90.2 versus 90.9 minutes**.

For each of the 200 Assist closures, apply the prior week’s mean responder minutes for its service group, severity, and intake channel. All 200 have a manual benchmark. This yields **200.9 benchmark hours versus 302.9 recorded hours**, a **102.0-hour excess**. Using severity alone or severity and service group gives the same result to the nearest hour. For sev1, the nine Assist closures each reopened within 72 hours and averaged 72 more responder minutes than manual sev1 closures. Five additional Assist sev1 incidents had no closure record. The extra work reported by responders is consistent with the sev1 evidence, and the increase in recorded labor also extends to lower severities.

Actual labor for the 11 missing activity records is unknown. As a sensitivity calculation, assigning zero minutes to missing activity in both periods and benchmarking all 210 Assist openings gives **78.0 excess recorded hours**. Filling missing labor with the same workflow and cell’s closed-case mean, using the same workflow’s sev1 mean for the two missing identity/customer sev1 records that have no Assist closures in their cell, gives **109.9 excess hours**. These scenarios illustrate the role of missing labor and do not bound the true or causal difference. With zero labor on all ten missing Assist cases, the one missing manual case would need about **2,173 minutes** to erase the all-opening standardized excess.

Raw handoffs fell from **2.25 to 1.96** per recorded closure. The manual benchmark falls to **1.31** after matching the Assist closure mix. Sev1 is an exception, with handoffs falling from **5.93 to 0.44** despite slower closure and **9 of 9** recorded closures reopening, versus **0 of 28** on manual. No other recorded closures reopened in either period. The latest recorded close allowed a full 72-hour observation window before extraction. The exports do not show what happened after reopening or whether handoff capture changed.

## What the pilot can establish

Assignment by opening time verifies which workflow an incident entered. The same rule makes workflow inseparable from calendar week in these data. Active responders increased from **12 to 14** per day in identity and **11 to 13** in storage, and total scheduled hours rose from **1,282 to 1,524**. Interruption minutes rose from **290 to 934**, with the same opening volume. Reweighting accounts for observed intake mix, but cannot isolate Assist from operating changes, differences in incident difficulty within severity tiers, or changes in recording. Staffing is a daily group snapshot and does not measure exposure or labor on each incident. Both groups switched together, and one week on each side gives little basis to estimate the recovery trend that would have continued under manual. The exports measure recorded closure, with reopening as a durability check. They contain no independent restoration timestamp.

Any further rollout should be a limited evaluation with a concurrent manual comparison and randomized assignment where operationally feasible. Capture responder minutes for open and closed incidents, track restoration and reopening, and judge the results by severity as well as in aggregate. Revisit expansion and the savings forecast when the comparison shows lower labor without deterioration in recovery or reopening, especially for sev1.
EOF
wc -w decision-memo.md"
